theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a monthly report on financial activity to a company's management?
options: To list every transaction recorded in the ledger that month
To meet the tax authority's rules for monthly tax filing
To show results against plan and what needs action
To take the place of the year-end financial statements

questions.stem: A finance officer reports to the board of a Kingston manufacturing company and to its department managers. How should the reports differ?
options: The board gets key results; managers get detail on their areas
The board gets every invoice; managers get only total profit
Both get the full ledger so that no one is ever left out
Managers get no figures, only a note of the board's decisions

questions.stem: Why does a finance team keep a month-end reporting timetable?
options: So the reports can go out whenever staff have the time
So each task is done in order and reports are on time
So the auditors can prepare the monthly management accounts
So the bank statements arrive earlier each month

questions.stem: Goods worth J$350,000 arrived and were used on 30 June, the last day of the month, but the supplier's invoice came on 5 July. What should the June report show?
options: Nothing for these goods until the invoice has been paid
The cost in July, the month in which the invoice arrived
Half of the cost in June and the other half in July
The cost in June, as an accrued expense

questions.stem: December's electricity bill has not arrived when the December report is prepared. Usage is estimated at J$85,000. What should be done?
options: Accrue J$85,000 as December's electricity cost
Leave electricity out of the December report
Charge the J$85,000 to January's report instead
Record the last bill paid, whatever its amount

questions.stem: A company whose year ends on 31 March pays J$1,200,000 on 1 January for 12 months' insurance. How much is an expense in the year to 31 March?
A company pays J$600,000 on 1 October for 12 months of security services. Its year ends on 31 December. How much is shown as a prepayment at 31 December?
Before the monthly report is issued, why should the bank, customer and supplier balances be reconciled?
options: To make the month's profit figure look a good deal higher
To confirm the balances are complete and correct
To avoid having to send the report for review
To reduce the GCT payable for the month

questions.stem: Which statement shows whether a business made a profit or a loss over a period?
options: The income statement (profit and loss account)
The statement of financial position (balance sheet)
The aged list of amounts owed by customers
The register of fixed assets and their costs

questions.stem: What does the statement of financial position show?
options: Income and expenses for the whole of the year
Cash received and paid out each month
Assets, liabilities and equity at a date
Sales by product line for the quarter

questions.stem: A company reports a good profit for the quarter, but its bank balance has fallen. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Profit and cash always move together, so there must be an error
Customers owe more, or cash went on stock, assets or loans
The profit figure must include the GCT collected from customers
The bank must have charged the wrong rate of interest on loans

questions.stem: A business starts the month with J$2,500,000 in the bank, receives J$8,400,000 and pays out J$9,100,000. What is its closing bank balance?
Which comparison makes a monthly financial report most useful to managers?
options: This month's actual figures alone, with no comparison at all
This month's figures against those reported by a competitor
Last year's budget against last year's audited accounts
Actual against budget and last year, for month and year to date

questions.stem: Budgeted repairs were J$400,000 and actual repairs were J$520,000. How should this be reported?
options: An adverse variance of J$120,000, or 30%
A favourable variance of J$120,000, or 30%
An adverse variance of J$120,000, or 23%
A favourable variance of J$520,000, or 130%

questions.stem: A juice maker budgeted to sell 10,000 cases at J$500 each. It sold 9,000 cases at J$540 each. What is the total sales variance?
options: J$360,000 favourable
J$500,000 adverse
J$140,000 adverse
J$140,000 favourable

questions.stem: A bakery budgeted to sell 10,000 cakes at J$500 each, but sold 9,000 cakes at J$540 each. What is the sales volume variance, valued at the budgeted price?
options: J$540,000 adverse
J$500,000 adverse
J$360,000 favourable
J$140,000 adverse

questions.stem: A company's policy asks for an explanation of any cost variance over 5% or over J$100,000. Which line needs an explanation?
options: Travel: budget J$1,800,000, actual J$1,926,000
Stationery: budget J$300,000, actual J$312,000
Cleaning: budget J$900,000, actual J$936,000
Postage: budget J$150,000, actual J$155,000

questions.stem: A delivery firm's fuel costs are 18% over budget for the quarter. What should the report writer do before writing the explanation?
options: Assume that fuel prices rose and write that in the report
Leave the line out, since fuel is hard for anyone to control
Spread the overspend across the other cost lines instead
Check the figures and ask the transport manager why

questions.stem: Which variance explanation is most useful to managers?
options: Costs were higher than the budget this month
Several things went wrong during the month
Overtime rose J$240,000 to cover two vacant posts
The variance is due to timing and other factors

questions.stem: A J$600,000 favourable variance on maintenance arose because work planned for May will now be done in July. How should it be reported?
options: As a permanent saving that can be spent on other things
As a timing difference that should reverse in July
As an error in the budget that ought to be deleted
As extra profit for the year, to be paid out as bonus

questions.stem: After nine months, a department has spent J$27,000,000 against a full-year budget of J$40,000,000. Spending is steady and is expected to stay so. What is the likely full-year outturn?
Why does a monthly report show year-to-date figures as well as the month's own figures?
options: To make the monthly figures look smaller than they are
So that the report can be much shorter than before
Because one month alone can mislead; the trend matters
Because the law requires every report to show them

questions.stem: A month-end stock count finds J$400,000 of goods damaged by flooding that cannot be sold. How should the report treat them?
options: Write the stock down and report the loss as a cost
Leave it in stock at cost until it can be sold
Move it into next year so as to protect profit
Add it to the value of the fixed assets instead

questions.stem: An aged debtors report shows that J$1,200,000 of the J$8,000,000 owed by customers is more than 90 days old. What share is that, and what should the report recommend?
options: 1.5%: no action of any kind is needed
15%: write all of it off at once
6.7%: stop selling to every customer
15%: chase these debts and review credit terms

questions.stem: Why should a financial report show the amounts owed to suppliers by age?
options: To show which suppliers the managers like the best
So that suppliers can be paid in alphabetical order
To plan payments and avoid late fees and supply problems
To avoid recording supplier invoices in the ledger

questions.stem: A hotel's report shows food costs at 42% of food sales against a target of 35%. Which option should the report suggest looking at first?
options: Portion control, waste, purchase prices and menu prices
Closing the restaurant for the rest of the financial year
Moving the food costs into the rooms department's figures
Cutting housekeeping staff to make up the difference

questions.stem: A report sets out three ways to recover a J$2,000,000 shortfall. How should the options be presented?
options: As one option only, so that the managers are not confused
As a list of ideas with no figures or comments of any kind
As whichever option the finance officer happens to like best
With each one's effect, cost, risk and timing, and a recommendation

questions.stem: Which order suits a written monthly financial report to a board?
options: Detailed tables first, then the appendices, then the summary
Summary, key results, variances, outlook, recommendations
Recommendations, then the raw ledger, then the summary
Bank statements, then the payroll, then the conclusions

questions.stem: Which visual best shows the board how monthly sales compared with budget across the year?
options: A line or column chart of actual and budget by month
A pie chart of the year's total sales split by month
A table of every single invoice issued in the year
A photo of the sales team at the year-end party

questions.stem: Before the monthly report goes to the board, who should review it?
options: Nobody, so that it reaches the board sooner
Any staff member in the office who has some free time
A senior finance person, who checks and signs it
The company's customers, to see if they agree

questions.stem: After the report was sent, the finance officer finds that a J$450,000 invoice was posted twice. What should she do?
options: Say nothing and quietly correct it next month
Tell her manager, correct it and send a note of the change
Ask the board members to destroy their copies of the report
Take the same amount off another cost line to balance it

questions.stem: The managing director asks the finance officer to hold back J$2,000,000 of December invoices so that the year's profit looks better. What should she do?
options: Do it, since the managing director is her senior
Do it, but only for invoices from small suppliers
Do it, and correct the position later in the year
Refuse, explain the rules and raise it as policy says

questions.stem: Why should monthly reports use the same accounting policies as the year-end accounts?
options: So that the monthly profit is always higher
So that the auditors need not check the accounts
So results can be compared and no surprises arise
So the reports can be prepared without a ledger

questions.stem: A finance officer's report uses figures exported from the accounting system into a spreadsheet. What should she check?
options: That the spreadsheet totals agree with the system's trial balance
That the spreadsheet uses the company's own colours and logo
That the export was done by the most senior person available
That all of the figures are rounded to the nearest million

questions.stem: A draft report shows a planned branch closure that staff have not yet been told about. How should it be handled?
options: Leave copies in the staff room so that staff can comment
Share it only with those entitled, and mark it confidential
Post the main points on all of the company's social media pages
E-mail it to all of the staff to save on printing costs

questions.stem: A charity in Montego Bay received a J$5,000,000 grant for a youth programme. What should its financial report to the funder show?
options: The charity's total spending on all of its programmes
Only the amount of the grant that is still in the bank
A letter of thanks with no figures attached to it
Spending against the agreed grant budget, explained

questions.stem: A government agency's quarterly financial report must go to its parent ministry. What should guide its content and timing?
options: The ministry's requirements and the public finance rules
The personal preference of the agency's newest finance clerk
Whatever the agency's suppliers would like to see in it
The format used by a private firm in the same street

questions.stem: A store's sales rose by 10% on budget, but its gross profit fell. What should the report investigate?
options: Whether the sales staff took all of their leave
Whether the office rent was paid on time each month
Changes in purchase prices, discounts and sales mix
Whether the bank charged interest on the loan

questions.stem: Administration costs are J$900,000 over budget. Which breakdown helps managers most?
options: A single total figure for all administration costs
A list of every staff member's name and grade
The same total figure shown in US dollars as well
The overspend split by cost line and by cause

questions.stem: Why are capital spending and day-to-day operating spending reported separately?
options: Capital spending never needs approval of any kind
Capital items last for years and are approved and tracked as such
Operating spending is never included in the profit for the year
Capital spending is only reported once every five years

questions.stem: A company buys a delivery van for J$6,000,000 to use for five years, with no value at the end. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the monthly charge in its reports?
A Jamaican firm owes a US supplier US$20,000. Before payment, the rate moves from J$155 to J$158 per US$. What is the effect on the amount owed in J$?
options: It falls by J$60,000
It rises by J$3,000
It rises by J$60,000
It does not change

questions.stem: Which point should a finance officer keep in mind when presenting the financial report at a board meeting?
options: Read every figure in the tables aloud from start to finish
Use as much technical accounting language as possible
Avoid taking questions so the meeting can finish early
Focus on key messages, risks and the decisions needed

questions.stem: The board agrees actions to deal with an overspend. What should the next month's report include?
options: No mention of the overspend, so as to avoid any embarrassment
Progress on the agreed actions and their financial effect
Only the figures, with all of the commentary removed
A new budget with the overspent line taken out of it

questions.stem: Managers say the monthly financial report is too long and arrives too late to act on. What should the finance manager do?
options: Ask users what they need, shorten it and speed up month-end
Add more tables so that nothing at all is ever missed out
Send it each quarter instead, without asking anyone first
Tell the managers to read it more carefully in future

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term names a cost that belongs to the period but has not yet been invoiced or paid, and is added to the period's accounts?
What term names a payment made in advance for a cost that belongs to a later period?
Budgeted sales were 5,000 units at J$800 each. Actual sales were 5,400 units at J$780 each. What is the sales price variance, in J$?
A company's year ends on 31 March. On 1 February it paid J$360,000 for 12 months of software licences. How much is the prepayment at 31 March, in J$?
What term names the rule that each transaction must be recorded in the period in which it belongs, at the boundary between two periods?
A guest house's bank account opened the month at J$1,200,000. It received J$5,600,000 from guests and paid J$6,100,000 to suppliers and staff. What did the account close at, in J$?
Budgeted staff training was J$250,000 and actual spending was J$200,000. What is the variance as a percentage of budget?
What word describes a variance where the actual result is worse than budget, such as costs above budget?
What term names the list of amounts owed by customers, sorted by how long each amount has been outstanding?
After six months, a department has spent J$15,000,000 at a steady rate that is expected to continue. What is the forecast full-year spend, in J$?
What two-word term describes improperly adjusting figures at a period end so that results look better than they really are?

A hotel buys laundry machines for J$2,400,000 and expects to use them for four years, after which they will be worth nothing. What yearly depreciation should its reports show on a straight-line basis, in J$?
What two-word term names the list of all ledger account balances, used to check that debits equal credits before reports are prepared?
What word names the level of a variance, such as 5% or J$100,000, above which a company's policy requires an explanation?
A firm owes a supplier US$10,000. Before payment, the rate rises from J$156 to J$160 per US$. By how much does the amount owed in J$ rise?

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would take at month-end to prepare an accurate financial report for a medium-sized distribution company.
essays.modelAnswer: I would work to a month-end timetable with a named owner and deadline for each task. First I would make sure all of the month's sales invoices, supplier invoices, payroll and cash were posted, applying cut-off so that goods delivered or received near the month-end fall in the right month. I would post accruals for costs incurred but not yet invoiced, such as electricity and goods received without an invoice, and release the right share of prepayments, such as insurance. Depreciation would be charged and stock counted or adjusted. Next I would reconcile the bank account, the customer and supplier control accounts and any suspense account, and clear or explain every difference. Once the trial balance agrees, I would extract the figures into the report template and check that its totals agree with the trial balance. I would compare the results with budget and last year, investigate significant variances with the managers involved and write the commentary. A senior finance person would review and sign off the report before it is sent, on time, to its users.
markingPoints: Works to a timetable with owners and deadlines
Completes postings and applies cut-off
Posts accruals, prepayments, depreciation and stock adjustments
Reconciles bank and control accounts and checks the report against the trial balance
Analyses variances, writes commentary and gets review and sign-off

essays.stem: A restaurant group's March figures show: sales J$12,000,000 against a budget of J$13,500,000; food cost J$4,560,000 against a budget of J$4,725,000; wages J$3,900,000 against a budget of J$3,600,000. Analyse these figures and explain what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: Sales were J$1,500,000 below budget, an adverse variance of about 11.1%. Food cost was J$165,000 below budget, which looks favourable, but this hides a problem. The budget set food cost at 35% of sales (J$4,725,000 out of J$13,500,000). Actual food cost was 38% of sales (J$4,560,000 out of J$12,000,000). At 35% of actual sales, food should have cost J$4,200,000, so food was about J$360,000 higher than it should have been for the sales made. Wages were J$300,000 over budget, an 8.3% adverse variance, even though sales fell; wages rose from about 26.7% to 32.5% of sales. Budgeted sales less food and wages was J$5,175,000; actual was J$3,540,000, a shortfall of J$1,635,000. I would report that the main problems are lower sales, higher food cost per sale and wages that did not fall with sales. I would ask managers about the causes, such as fewer covers, price rises from suppliers, waste or overtime, and recommend actions on promotion, portion control, purchasing and rosters.
markingPoints: Calculates the sales variance correctly (J$1,500,000 adverse, about 11.1%)
Shows that food cost rose from 35% to 38% of sales despite the lower total
Calculates the wages variance (J$300,000 adverse) and its rise as a share of sales
Works out the combined shortfall of J$1,635,000
Suggests causes to investigate and sensible actions

essays.stem: The board of a growing company asks why it made a profit of J$8,000,000 this year while its bank overdraft grew. Explain how you would answer in your report.
essays.modelAnswer: I would explain that profit and cash are measured differently. Profit matches income earned with the costs of earning it, whether or not cash has moved, while the cash position shows what was actually received and paid. I would prepare a short statement of cash flows to link the two. It would start with the J$8,000,000 profit, add back depreciation, which reduces profit but uses no cash, and then show the effect of changes in working capital. A growing company often sells more on credit, so customers owe more at the year end; it may hold more stock, and it may pay suppliers faster. Each of these uses cash. I would then show capital spending, such as new vehicles or equipment, loan repayments and any dividends paid, which do not appear as costs in the income statement but take cash. The report would show which items caused the overdraft to grow, using the figures, and recommend actions, such as tighter credit control, lower stock levels, funding capital spending with a suitable loan and a monthly cash forecast.
markingPoints: Explains the difference between profit and cash
Links them with a cash flow statement starting from profit
Shows the effect of working capital: receivables, stock and payables
Includes capital spending, loan repayments and dividends
Recommends actions such as credit control, stock control, funding and cash forecasting

essays.stem: At the half year, a distribution company's profit is 20% below budget, mainly because of lower sales margins and higher transport costs. Evaluate options to improve its financial performance and make a recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: One option is to raise selling prices on lines where margins have fallen. This acts quickly, but customers may buy less or move to competitors, so it should be tested on lines where the company has a strong position. A second option is to buy better, by negotiating with suppliers, buying in larger lots or changing suppliers; this protects prices but may take time and tie up cash in stock. A third option is to cut transport costs by planning routes better, combining deliveries, setting minimum order values or charging for small deliveries; this can save money without upsetting most customers, though some may object to delivery charges. A fourth is to cut overheads, which can help, but cutting too deeply may harm service. For each option I would estimate the effect on profit, the cost, the risks and how quickly it would work. I would recommend combining route planning and minimum order values, which are low-risk and quick, with supplier negotiations and selected price rises, and report progress against a revised forecast each month.
markingPoints: Evaluates price rises with their risks
Evaluates buying better or changing suppliers
Evaluates cutting transport costs through routes and order policies
Considers overheads and weighs effect, cost, risk and timing
Makes a justified, combined recommendation with monitoring

essays.stem: Describe how you would structure and present a monthly financial report so that a board can understand it and act on it quickly.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin with a one-page summary that gives the key messages in plain words: profit against budget and last year, the cash position, the main risks and the decisions the board is asked to make. Next would come a short table of key results for the month and year to date, showing actual, budget, last year and the variances in J$ and per cent, with a simple colour code for lines that need attention. A commentary would explain only the significant variances, as set by the company's threshold, giving the cause, whether it is timing or permanent, and the action being taken. I would add one or two clear charts, such as monthly sales against budget and the cash balance trend. A section on the outlook would give the forecast for the full year and the main risks. Recommendations would be numbered and specific. Detailed statements would go in appendices for those who want them. I would use consistent layouts each month, label all figures and units, avoid jargon and send the report early enough for board members to read it before the meeting.
markingPoints: Opens with a short summary of key messages and decisions needed
Shows key results against budget and last year, for the month and year to date
Explains significant variances with causes and actions
Uses clear charts, an outlook and specific recommendations
Keeps detail in appendices, uses a consistent layout and sends it in good time

essays.stem: Explain how you would report on a company's working capital each month, and what actions such a report might lead to.
essays.modelAnswer: Working capital is the money tied up in stock and amounts owed by customers, less the amounts owed to suppliers. I would report each part every month. For receivables, I would show the total owed, debtor days against target and an aged debtors analysis, highlighting customers with large or very old balances. For stock, I would show the value held, stock days or turnover, and slow-moving or obsolete items. For payables, I would show the total owed, creditor days and any overdue supplier accounts. I would show the trend over several months and compare each measure with target, and link it to the cash forecast so managers see the effect on the bank balance. Actions might include chasing overdue accounts, stopping further credit to customers over their limit, reviewing credit terms, offering early payment discounts, cutting reorder levels for slow lines and clearing old stock, and agreeing better payment terms with suppliers without damaging relationships. The report would track whether these actions were taken and whether the figures improved.
markingPoints: Explains what working capital is
Reports receivables with debtor days and an aged analysis
Reports stock and payables with suitable measures
Shows trends and links them to the cash forecast
Identifies sensible actions and tracks their results

essays.stem: Explain why integrity matters in financial reporting, and how a finance officer should respond to pressure to make results look better than they are.
essays.modelAnswer: Managers, boards, lenders, funders and the tax authority rely on financial reports to make decisions. If figures are adjusted to look better, such as holding back invoices, not recording accruals, overstating stock or moving costs between periods, decisions will be based on false information. Problems are hidden until they become worse, lenders and funders may be misled, and the organisation may break company law, tax rules or the terms of its loans and grants. The finance officer's own professional standing and job are also at risk. If pressured, the officer should stay calm and polite, explain the accounting rules and the risks, and offer an honest alternative, such as explaining the poor result clearly and suggesting actions. The officer should keep a written note of the request and the response. If the pressure continues, the officer should raise it with a more senior person, the audit committee or through the whistle-blowing policy, as the organisation's policy sets. The officer must not make the change, even if told to by a senior manager.
markingPoints: Explains who relies on reports and the harm from misleading figures
Gives examples of improper adjustments
Notes the legal, contractual and professional risks in general terms
Responds by explaining the rules and offering honest alternatives
Records the request and escalates through the proper channels without making the change

essays.stem: Compare reporting financial activity to a company's board with reporting to an outside funder or a parent ministry, and explain how you would meet each one's needs.
essays.modelAnswer: A company board wants to know how the whole business is doing against its budget and strategy, what the main risks are and what decisions it must make. Its report covers profit, cash, working capital and the forecast, with commentary on significant variances, and its format is set by the company. An outside funder, such as a donor or a development agency, wants to know whether its grant was spent on what was agreed, within the agreed budget lines and time. Its report must follow the funder's template and dates, show spending against the grant budget, explain any variances, and often include receipts or an audit. A parent ministry wants assurance that a public body is using public money properly and within its approved budget, in line with the public finance rules, and it sets the format and timetable. In each case I would first find out the user's requirements and deadlines, keep records that can be traced to each report, explain variances honestly, and make sure figures agree with the accounts. I would keep a reporting calendar so that no report is late.
markingPoints: Describes a board's needs and report content
Describes an outside funder's needs and report content
Describes a parent ministry's needs and the public finance rules in general terms
Follows each user's requirements and deadlines
Keeps traceable records, honest explanations and a reporting calendar

essays.stem: Explain how you would prepare and report a forecast of the year-end result (the outturn) in the middle of the financial year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the actual results for the year to date, checked and reconciled. For each main line of income and cost, I would then forecast the remaining months rather than simply assume the budget will be met. For steady costs, such as rent, the budget or the current monthly rate may be fine. For other lines, I would ask the managers responsible about known changes: new contracts, lost customers, price rises, vacant posts, planned projects and seasonal patterns, such as the tourist season or Christmas. Timing differences from earlier months would be put back in the months they are now expected. I would add the actual and forecast figures to give the full-year outturn and compare it with the budget and last year. The report would show the forecast, the main changes since the last forecast and the key assumptions, and set out the risks and opportunities, perhaps with a best and worst case. If the outturn shows a shortfall, I would set out options to close the gap. I would update the forecast each month or quarter.
markingPoints: Starts from checked year-to-date actuals
Forecasts each line for the remaining months using manager input and known changes
Allows for seasonality and timing differences
Reports the outturn against budget with assumptions, risks and scenarios
Proposes actions for any gap and updates the forecast regularly

essays.stem: Managers at a statutory body say the monthly financial reports come too late and are too long to be useful. Recommend how the reporting process could be improved.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first ask the main users what decisions they make, what information they need and when, and review the current timetable to find the slowest steps. I would then agree a shorter month-end timetable, for example a report by the eighth working day, with clear owners and deadlines. To speed things up, I would post regular accruals and prepayments from a schedule, reconcile bank and control accounts weekly, ask departments to send invoices before the month-end, and use the accounting system's reports or a linked template instead of retyping figures. The report itself would be cut to a one-page summary, a key results table with the month, the year to date and the forecast, short commentary on variances above the threshold, and a few charts, with the detail in appendices. Each department would get a short report on its own area. Checks, such as agreeing the template to the trial balance and a senior review, would stay in place so that speed does not cost accuracy. After three months I would ask users for feedback and adjust the process again.
markingPoints: Finds out users' needs and the causes of delay
Sets a shorter timetable with owners and deadlines
Speeds up month-end through schedules, regular reconciliations and less retyping
Shortens the report and tailors it to users
Keeps accuracy checks and reviews the changes with users

practical1.title: Prepare a monthly financial activity report from the trial balance and budget
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for a made-up Jamaican company (for example a building supplies distributor in May Pen): the month's trial balance, the budget and last year's figures for the month and year to date, and notes on items not yet recorded (an unpaid electricity bill, an insurance payment covering 12 months, and goods received without an invoice). As a group, prepare the month's financial report for the board. Give each member a named role: adjustments officer (works out and lists the accruals and prepayment adjustments and their effect on profit, checking every figure twice), analyst (builds a spreadsheet table of actual, budget and last year for the month and year to date, with variances in J$ and per cent, and marks the lines over the company's threshold), commentary writer (writes a short explanation of each significant variance, stating whether it is timing or permanent), chart maker (makes two clear charts, such as sales against budget by month and the cash balance), and report lead (writes the one-page summary with recommendations and checks that the report's totals agree with the trial balance). In a group of four, the report lead also makes the charts.
materials: Data pack with trial balance, budget, last year's figures and notes from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word processor software
photos: The list of adjustments with workings
The spreadsheet on screen with actual, budget, last year and variances
The one-page summary with recommendations, and the check against the trial balance
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the report
Accrual and prepayment adjustments are correct and were checked twice
Variances are correct in J$ and per cent, and the right lines are marked for explanation
Commentary gives causes, separates timing from permanent differences and suggests actions
Charts are suitable, labelled and honest
Report totals agree with the trial balance and the summary is clear
safety: Treat the data pack as confidential financial information; return all printouts to the assessor
Use made-up names for the company and its people
Report the figures honestly, even when the results are poor
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break

practical2.title: Investigate variances, forecast the outturn and present options at a management meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a half-year report for a made-up organisation (for example a hotel in Negril or a municipal corporation's revenue department) showing a shortfall against budget, with cards giving information from department heads about the causes. As a group, investigate, forecast and present. Give each member a named role: investigator (questions the department heads, played by the assessor or another trainee, using the cards, and records the causes of each main variance), forecaster (prepares a full-year outturn forecast in a spreadsheet with stated assumptions, checking every figure twice), options analyst (sets out at least three options to improve the result with their effect, cost, risk and timing), report writer (writes a two-page report with the findings, forecast, options and a recommendation), and presenter (leads a 15-minute role-played management meeting with the assessor as the general manager, with help from the others). In a group of four, the options analyst also presents.
materials: Half-year report and department head cards from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet, word processor and presentation software
photos: The investigator's notes of causes for each main variance
The outturn forecast spreadsheet with assumptions
The options table with effect, cost, risk and timing
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the work
Causes of variances come from the evidence gathered, not guesses
Forecast is correct, with clear and reasonable assumptions
Options are evaluated fairly, with figures, and the recommendation is justified
Report is clear, honest and well organised
Answered the general manager's questions calmly and with evidence
safety: Treat the report and cards as confidential; return them to the assessor
Keep questioning of department heads polite and focused on facts, not blame
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break
